subject: Section 8 pays 10-18% above market in some zip codes
preheader: FMR often beats market rent in B/C zones · the screening trade-off · why the data doesn't match the stereotypes

marketSnapshot.headline: Section 8 — the honest math under the stereotypes
marketSnapshot.body: Section 8 housing vouchers pay a 'Fair Market Rent' (FMR) set annually by HUD per metro zone. In many B and C-tier neighborhoods, FMR is meaningfully above the open-market rent — sometimes 10-20% above. Investors who avoid Section 8 due to perception are often leaving real return on the table. The trade-off is real (annual HQS inspections, longer placement, more paperwork) but the rent premium absorbs most of the friction in voucher-favorable zones.

stats.label: Typical FMR premium in qualifying zones

dealSpotter.body: B-tier Midwest property. Market rent $1,275. Section 8 FMR for a 3-bedroom: $1,485. The 16% premium covers the inspection prep cost, the placement delay, and even pads in some tolerance for damaged-unit repair on turnover. The HUD-paid portion arrives like clockwork. The tenant portion (the rent above what the voucher covers, if any) is the only piece you collect privately.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 1.8% premium · friction not worth it · Decent (skip voucher)
dealSpotter.body: In zones where market rents have caught up to FMR, the voucher premium evaporates and the friction stops being worth it. Don't accept voucher just because you can — calculate the premium first. If it's <5%, market-rate rentals win on net economics.

Some A-tier neighborhoods have FMRs that lag market rents — common in fast-appreciating zones. If FMR pays less than market, voucher tenants take a discount. The economics for landlords work in the opposite direction. Don't accept vouchers in these zones; you're leaving money on the table.

blogFeature.title: The 50% rule for rentals — still useful in 2026?
blogFeature.excerpt: The 50% rule says expenses run 50% of gross rent. For Section 8 properties, the expense ratio is usually higher (inspection prep, slightly more turnover work). Useful for triage; dangerous as a substitute for a real underwrite.

qa.question: Are voucher tenants statistically worse renters than market-rate tenants?
qa.answer: No — controlling for the comparable price band. The bias is comparing voucher tenants to A-tier market-rate tenants, which isn't the right comparison. Compare voucher tenants to the bottom 30% of market-rate tenants in the same neighborhood and the data shows voucher tenants do equal or better on payment reliability (because the housing authority pays the bulk, not the tenant) and similar on property care. Where voucher tenants underperform: turnover frequency tends to be slightly higher (life-stage instability) and inspection prep costs you a few hundred dollars a year per unit. Where they outperform: payment reliability, longer-than-expected tenancies in good cases (5-10 year voucher tenancies are common), and lower vacancy-driven income variability. The 'lazy bias' worth setting aside is treating voucher status as a proxy for tenant quality. Screening matters; the voucher itself is mostly orthogonal to outcome.
